summary: This informational document presents thoughts on how supporting HTTP Adaptive Streaming (HAS) affects Content Distribution Network Interconnection (CDNI). It gives the authors' analysis of the problem space and options for handling HAS in CDNI. It was used as input in the CDNI working group.

plainLanguage.summary: HTTP Adaptive Streaming splits a video into many small pieces and lets the player change quality as the network speed changes. This RFC asks what that does to CDNI, the set of interfaces that let separate content delivery networks work together. It compares the options for storing, fetching, logging and protecting the pieces, and recommends keeping the interfaces as they are for now.

questions: what is a manifest file in streaming
how does url signing work with adaptive streaming
subtitle: What HTTP Adaptive Streaming does to the interfaces that let separate content delivery networks work together.

tldr.problem: CDNI lets one content delivery network hand a request to another. HTTP Adaptive Streaming does not fit the shape CDNI was designed around, because a video arrives as many small pieces and a list describing where those pieces live.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC walks through how streaming content is chunked, stored and addressed, then works through six problem areas: file management, content acquisition, request routing, logging, URL signing and content purge. For each it lists options and states which one the authors recommend.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational RFC written as input to the CDNI working group. The overall recommendation is to make streaming work with the interfaces as they are, and to defer the optimisations that would need interface extensions or streaming awareness in the downstream CDN.

today: RFC 6983 is an Informational RFC published in July 2013. It has not been obsoleted or updated. It was written as input to the CDNI working group's decision on HTTP Adaptive Streaming support, not as a specification of the CDNI interfaces themselves.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 6707 defines the problem space for Content Distribution Network Interconnection and the associated CDNI interfaces, including the support, through interconnected content delivery networks, of content delivery to end users using HTTP progressive download and HTTP Adaptive Streaming.

HTTP Adaptive Streaming is an umbrella term for HTTP-based streaming technologies that let a client switch between several bitrates depending on current network conditions. Its defining property is that, because it is built on HTTP, it is a pull-based mechanism: the client actively requests the content segments instead of the content being pushed to it by a server. That pull-based nature gives media servers delivering HAS content different characteristics from media servers using traditional streaming methods such as RTP/RTSP, RTMP and MMS.

The document presents the impact of HAS on the CDNI interfaces and the HAS-specific optimisations that may be required or may be desirable. Its scope is the authors' analysis of the problem space and a discussion of the options put forward by the authors and by others during informal discussions. The aim is to make streaming work, rather than to include nice-to-have optimisations that might delay the working group's deliverables.

The document is explicit about what it is not. It is not a working group document, but it was used as input during the working group process for the decision on HAS support. The Security Considerations section is a single sentence: the document does not discuss security issues related to HTTP or HAS delivery, because those topics are expected to be covered in the CDNI working group documents.
sections.plainLanguage: CDNI is a set of interfaces that let one content delivery network pass work to another. Streaming breaks the shape those interfaces were built around. This RFC compares the options and recommends keeping the interfaces as they are for now.

sections.title: The Vocabulary of HAS Content
sections.content:
The RFC restates the terms it needs, and they describe a nesting of things.

A content item is a uniquely addressable element in a CDN, defined by having its own content metadata. A video file or stream, an audio file or stream, or an image file are examples. A chunk is a fixed-length element produced by a segmentation or fragmentation operation and independently addressable. A chunk comes in two forms: a fragment, which is stored as part of a larger file that includes all the chunks of the chunk collection, and a segment, which is stored as a single file from a file-system point of view.

Original content is the non-chunked content that the segmentation or fragmentation operation is performed on. From it, several alternative representations can be derived, using different encodings, supporting different resolutions or targeting different bitrates, and each of those may then be fragmented or segmented. A chunk collection is the set of all chunks resulting from one such operation on one representation of the original content. A content collection is the set of all chunk collections derived from the same original content.

A manifest file, also called a Media Presentation Description or MPD, lists the way the content has been chunked and where the chunks are located, in the case of segments, or how they can be addressed, in the case of fragments. A content collection may be described by one or more manifest files, and a manifest file may also identify the different representations available.
sections.plainLanguage: One video becomes several versions. Each version is cut into chunks, and the chunks of one version form a chunk collection. A manifest file tells the player where the chunks are.

sections.title: Storing and Addressing HAS Content
sections.content:
Every HAS implementation is built on chunking: a server splits the content into numerous fixed-duration chunks that are independently decodable, and the client recreates the content by requesting them in order. The advantage is that a client can switch between different encodings of the same original content at chunk boundaries, choosing between alternative encodings for each chunk independently of the chunks it has already received.

Not all implementations store the chunks in the same way. With segmentation, which was mandatory in all versions of Apple's HLS prior to version 7, each chunk is a separate file and has its own unique URL. With fragmentation, used for example by Microsoft's HTTP Smooth Streaming, all the chunks of a chunk collection are stored together in one file, usually a fragmented MP4 container, and a specific chunk is addressed by adding an identifier to the common file URL, by timestamp, by byte range or in some other way. The RFC notes that fragmentation is often regarded as introducing less overhead from a storage and processing point of view, while segmentation is regarded as more flexible and easier to cache. Current implementations increasingly support both.

A client learns where the chunks are from the manifest file, and the RFC describes three ways the manifest file can point at them. Relative URLs carry only part of the path, and the client appends them to the location it fetched the manifest file from, so every chunk comes from the same surrogate that served the manifest file. That is easy to move between surrogates and CDNs, but it limits flexibility and leaves no fallback if that surrogate fails. Absolute URLs with redirection point at the CDN's request routing function, which then redirects the client to the surrogate it chooses; that allows the chunks to be spread anywhere, but adds request routing load for every chunk. Absolute URLs without redirection point straight at the surrogate holding the chunk, which avoids the redirection but means the manifest file has to be rewritten whenever the content moves.

Two situations complicate the picture. For live content the chunks and their manifest files are created in real time, so bundling and pre-positioning have little time to help, the manifest file has to be updated for each chunk and fetched before each chunk request, and its cacheability is limited. For stream splicing, where content from several sources is combined into a mashup, for example to insert advertisements, clients and proxies may rely on non-URL information in the manifest file. Any scheme that generates or rewrites manifest files has to leave chunk URLs, nested manifest file URLs and other metadata alone, or playback breaks and revenue is lost.
sections.plainLanguage: Chunks can be stored as separate files or packed into one file. The manifest file can point at them with a relative path, with a path that redirects first, or with a direct path to the server. Each way trades flexibility against overhead.

sections.title: File Management, Acquisition, Routing and Purge
sections.content:
The RFC works through six problem areas. For file management it asks how the CDNI interfaces should handle content collections, which are groups of interrelated files rather than a single file. Option 1.1 is to do nothing, so the downstream CDN stores chunks as individual files and needs no HAS awareness. Option 1.2 lets it store fragmented content as a single file, which cuts file management overhead but requires the downstream CDN to be fully HAS aware and needs new metadata fields. Option 1.3 adds an Access Correlation Hint to the metadata of all chunks in a collection, so the downstream CDN can bundle files without knowing anything about HAS. The authors recommend Option 1.1, because the benefit of Option 1.3 is too small to justify changing the metadata interface and Option 1.2 would delay the working group's milestones.

For content acquisition the options are similar. Option 2.1, no HAS awareness, means each file of a collection is acquired separately, which is flexible and saves bandwidth when a client only wants part of the content, but creates more transaction overhead between the CDNs. Option 2.2 allows single-file acquisition of fragmented content, which is more efficient but needs full HAS awareness in the downstream CDN and significant metadata extensions. The authors recommend Option 2.1.

For request routing, only absolute URLs with redirection work without question when neither CDN is HAS aware, and the price is a lot of signalling: the full inter-CDN request routing process runs for every chunk. Option 3.2 has the upstream CDN rewrite the manifest file so that it points straight at the downstream CDN's request routing function, which removes a redirect from the chain without changing the CDNI interfaces, at the cost of HAS awareness in the upstream CDN. Option 3.3 lets the downstream CDN rewrite the manifest file itself, in a second step, so it can use absolute URLs without redirection without having to reveal its surrogate locations; that needs HAS awareness downstream and new metadata fields. The authors recommend Option 3.1 with Option 3.2 as an optional CDN-internal behaviour, and advise against Option 3.3.

For content purge, the straightforward method is to send one purge request per file in the collection. Option 6.2 instead puts a Purge Identifier in the metadata of the files, the same value for every file of a content item and different across items, so a single purge request can name a whole collection. The authors recommend making the straightforward method mandatory and Purge Identifiers an optional extra.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC compares ways to store, fetch, route and delete streaming content across two CDNs. In each case the simplest option needs no change to the interfaces, and that is what the authors recommend.

sections.title: Logging at Scale
sections.content:
The CDNI Logging interface lets interconnected CDNs exchange log records, and those records serve maintenance and debugging, accounting and billing, reporting on end-user experience, analytics, and control of content distribution policy. HAS changes the scale of the problem: the number of log records can grow by two to three orders of magnitude, because records would typically be generated per chunk delivery instead of per content item. Every step of the logging process scales with it, from generating and storing records on surrogates and request routers, through aggregation, manipulation, reformatting and exchange, to the applications that consume the logs.

Four options are compared. Option 4.1, do nothing, sends a log record for every chunk delivery. Nothing is lost and existing logging tools can handle it, but every step has to cope with the volume, and summarising later is hard without hints in the records for correlating them. Option 4.2 distributes a Content Collection IDentifier through the metadata so that every chunk of a collection carries the same value, and optionally a Session IDentifier as well, which lets a downstream CDN group per-chunk records into per-session records without losing any detail. Option 4.3 compresses the log files for transfer, which shrinks only the transfer step. Option 4.4 assumes HAS awareness across the CDNs, so that the downstream CDN can summarise records as it generates them or correlate them afterwards; it lowers the volume at every step but needs significant interface extensions, specific support for every HAS protocol, and it loses some detail.

The authors recommend per-chunk logging as a mandatory capability and a high priority item, the Content Collection IDentifier and Session IDentifier mechanisms as an optional capability of medium priority, a generic mechanism for customising which log fields are reported, and common compression techniques such as gzip as another optional medium priority item. They advise against Option 4.4 for now, and suggest that a pull-style interface that lets the upstream CDN request the detail lost in summarised records would be worth investigating at a future rechartering.
sections.plainLanguage: Streaming produces one log record per chunk instead of one per video, so the volume can grow a hundredfold or more. The RFC compares ways to handle that and recommends logging every chunk, with identifiers that let the logs be grouped later.

sections.title: URL Signing
sections.content:
URL signing is an authorisation method for content delivery. The HTTP URL carries information that can be validated to confirm the request has legitimate access: parameters that convey authorisation restrictions such as a source IP address and a time period, or a protected portion of the URL, plus a message digest that confirms the integrity of the URL and authenticates whoever created it. A key produces the digest and checks it, either an asymmetric key pair or one symmetric key used for both jobs. The content owner signs the URL and gives it to the user during website navigation; when the user selects it, the CDN validates the URL before delivering the content.

HAS changes the lifetime problem. The expiry time in the signing parameters limits how long the referenced content can be accessed, which works for a URL that points straight at the media. For HAS content the manifest file holds another layer of URLs pointing at the chunks, and a chunk URL may be requested an undetermined amount of time later. The gap between fetching the manifest file and retrieving the chunk varies a lot, and the type of content, live or on demand, affects it too.

For CDNI the choice of key type affects the trust model. With DNS-based request routing the URL does not change, and a symmetric key has to be distributed from the authoritative CDN to the delivering CDN, which is awkward when the delivering CDN has no relationship with the content provider. With HTTP-based request routing the URL changes at each redirect, and each CDN in the chain signs the new URL with its own key.

Six options are compared. Option 5.1 signs only the top-level manifest file, leaving the lower-level manifest files and chunks unprotected, which the authors call unsuitable for access control. Option 5.2 has the content provider sign the chunk URLs as well, generating manifest files per session, which protects everything but makes the manifest files uncacheable and cannot work for absolute URLs with redirection over HTTP. Option 5.3 moves that job to the upstream CDN. Option 5.4 pairs a signed top-level manifest file with an HTTP cookie carrying the session state for the chunks, so the CDN needs no HAS awareness and the manifest files are not rewritten. Options 5.5 and 5.6 make the CDNs themselves HAS aware, using a cookie or by generating and rewriting manifest files.

The authors recommend Option 5.4 where the targeted user agents support HTTP cookies and the security requirements can be met that way, since it needs no manifest file manipulation. Otherwise they recommend flexible URL signing under Option 5.2 or 5.3. Options 5.5 and 5.6 are worth considering later, but making the CDNs HAS aware in the current charter would delay the working group's milestones.
sections.plainLanguage: URL signing puts a signed expiry into the link so the CDN can check that the viewer is allowed to have the content. Streaming makes this harder, because the video chunks are fetched later through URLs listed inside another file. The RFC compares six ways to handle that.

items.title: File management
items.text: Option 1.1, do nothing: the downstream CDN stores chunks as individual files.

items.title: Content acquisition
items.text: Option 2.1, no HAS awareness: each file is acquired separately.

items.title: Request routing
items.text: Option 3.1, with Option 3.2 as an optional CDN-internal behaviour.

items.title: Logging
items.text: Option 4.1, per-chunk logging, as a mandatory capability.

items.title: URL signing
items.text: Option 5.4 with an HTTP cookie, or flexible signing under Option 5.2 or 5.3.

items.title: Content purge
items.text: Option 6.1, do nothing, with Purge Identifiers as an optional extra.
